extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and educated readers interested in logic, probability, and scientific reasoning
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and formal principles for assessing the probability, strength, and combination of inductive arguments and scientific hypotheses; includes philosophical cautions about premises and formal rules for computing probabilities and aggregating evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise completeness and caution in extrapolation
rubrics_metrics.description: Premises in truth and completeness are of much more account and far more difficult of discovery than methods of logical inference; one should not mistake a provisional opinion for a final judgment or pronounce sweeping conclusions when important facts remain unknown.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The essay repeatedly warns against taking provisional summings-up as final—e.g., criticizing grand cosmological conclusions (the 'death' of the universe) drawn from incomplete premises. The author advises comparing the student to a judge who must await more witnesses before pronouncing sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume finiteness of matter or space without evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid assuming as a premise that matter and motion are finite in amount or that space has bounds when reasoning about cosmological consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The critique of the dissipation-of-energy theory notes the theory assumes finiteness of matter/motion; we cannot know or imagine bounds of space or the extent of orbs and movements, so such an assumption weakens sweeping conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume heat is absolutely homogeneous motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Question the premise that heat is an absolutely homogeneous motion (i.e., perfectly uniform thermal motion) — microscopic motions likely have structure that could serve as sources of mechanical change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author points to atomic structure and possible axial rotations or orbital motions of atoms which would produce non-homogeneous thermal motion; analogies with electricity and magnetism (cumulative toward poles) are offered as reasons to doubt perfect thermal homogeneity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for coexisting forms of energy and their interactions
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that heat often coexists with other phases of energy (chemical, gravitational, cohesive/crystalline), so thermal production need not be purely 'thermal' in its consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: heating changes dimensions (affecting gravity), decomposition of compounds at high temperature introduces chemical energy, and thermal effects can be pitted against cohesive forces. These interactions argue against the notion that all energy will end as uniformly diffused heat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present inability to perform a conversion does not prove impossibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Current failure or ignorance (e.g., inability to derive macroscopic work from uniformly heated matter) is not proof that conversion is impossible in Nature or for future science.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author urges intellectual humility: the impossibility conclusion is unwarranted given our limited knowledge of atomic structure and modes of motion; future discoveries may enable conversions now thought impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability defined as relative frequency of antecedent–consequent co-occurrence
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of a consequence is the number of times antecedent and consequent both occur divided by the number of times the antecedent occurs (material/frequency definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This definition underlies the subsequent formal rules; Peirce illustrates with dice examples to show how to compute probabilities from equally frequent cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for addition of probabilities (incompatible consequents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the separate probabilities of two consequences having the same antecedent and incompatible consequents, the sum of these two numbers is the probability that one or the other consequent follows from that antecedent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated via dice: probability of either of two mutually exclusive outcomes equals the sum of their separate probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule for multiplication of probabilities (chained consequents)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given probabilities for 'If A then B' and 'If both A and B then C', the product of these two numbers is the probability of 'If A then both B and C'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to compute probabilities for sequential/conditional events; illustrated with successive dice events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special multiplication rule for independent probabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: For two consequences with the same antecedent that are such that the probability of the second equals the probability of the consequence 'If both A and B then C', the product of the two probabilities equals the probability of 'If A then both B and C' (i.e., independent-consequence multiplication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the common rule that independent probabilities multiply; Peirce demonstrates by example with dice and with combining independent rules of inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish materialistic (frequency) and conceptualistic (degree-of-belief) views of probability
rubrics_metrics.description: Be explicit whether probability is treated as a matter of fact (materialistic: relative frequency) or as the degree of belief that should attach to a proposition (conceptualistic); mixing these without clarity introduces confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peirce discusses how most writers mix both views and emphasizes the importance of understanding the distinction when interpreting probability and when relating probability to belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'chance' (ratio favorable:unfavorable) and 'probability' appropriately; measure belief by chance-derived quantity
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce 'chance' as the ratio of favorable to unfavorable cases (distinct from probability) and relate belief intensity to a monotone function of chance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peirce prefers 'chance' as favorable:unfavorable ratio and argues that belief intensity should vary with chance; this sets up the choice of logarithm as an appropriate scale for belief intensity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure belief intensity as the logarithm of chance (additive property)
rubrics_metrics.description: Represent the intensity of belief by the logarithm of the chance of the event, because (a) belief intensity should go to infinity as chance goes to infinity and vanish at even chance, and (b) logarithms convert multiplication of chances (independent arguments) into addition of belief intensities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peirce invokes Fechner's psychophysical law to support the logarithmic scale and demonstrates with algebra that the product rule for independent arguments corresponds to additive combination of log-chances, which models how independent pieces of evidence should sum to yield overall belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine independent concurrent arguments by multiplying chances or adding log-beliefs
rubrics_metrics.description: For independent arguments, the combined chance is the product of the individual chances; equivalently, convert chances to log-belief intensities and add them to get the combined intensity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peirce gives numerical examples (e.g., two rules yielding correct answers with certain percentages) to show how combined agreement raises the probability that the common result is correct and shows the product-of-chances / sum-of-logs relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance pro and con arguments by summing their belief intensities
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiple independent arguments exist both for and against a proposition, the overall intensity of belief should be the sum of the intensities from pro arguments minus the sum from con arguments (i.e., balancing reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peirce recommends summing intensities (log-chances) for pro arguments, subtracting the sum for con arguments, and taking the remainder as the rational degree of belief; he notes this is already practiced informally as 'balancing reasons.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability and chance are relative to premises; evaluate consequences with respect to their antecedents
rubrics_metrics.description: Probability and chance pertain primarily to consequences relative to given premises (antecedents); thus probability assessments must specify the antecedent premises against which the consequent is measured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peirce emphasizes that probabilities belong to consequences and are relative to premises; when people speak of the absolute chance of an event they mean the chance considering the totality of arguments available in the current state of knowledge.
